raw_findings.message: `transferFrom()` deducts allowance before `_move()` can return false for insufficient balance, so a failed transfer still consumes the spender's allowance.
The constructor permits the staking and reward tokens to be identical, so reward payouts can spend tokens backing users' principal and leave withdrawals insolvent.
When rewards are active with no stake, `rewardPerToken()` divides by zero; for example, the first `stake()` after an epoch starts reverts in its `updateReward` modifier.
Dividing before applying the 1e18 scale truncates small per-token rewards to zero, so users can receive no accrual even when rewards were scheduled.
A new notification resets the global accumulator while users retain their larger prior paid value, so `earned()` wraps the subtraction and reports a huge incorrect reward.
The first deposit leaves `lockEnd` at zero, allowing a staker to withdraw immediately instead of being subject to the lockup.
The stake balance and total supply are unchanged until after the external token transfer, so an opted-in receiver hook can reenter `emergencyWithdraw()` and withdraw the same stake repeatedly.
`getReward()` ignores a false return from the reward token and has already cleared the user's rewards, so an underfunded payout silently destroys the user's claim.
The signed digest has no nonce or contract/chain domain, so anyone can reuse a valid voucher to claim the bonus repeatedly.
Any account can call `notifyRewardAmount()` and replace the active reward schedule, letting an attacker disrupt the owner's intended distribution.
Starting a new epoch replaces the current rate without carrying forward its unelapsed rewards, so re-notifying before the prior period ends abandons the remaining scheduled distribution.
Integer division makes `rewardRate` zero whenever `reward < duration`, leaving the funded reward undistributed for the entire epoch.

`_move` accepts `address(0)` as the recipient, so a successful transfer can leave tokens irretrievably assigned to the zero address without reducing `totalSupply`.

raw_findings.message: transferFrom reduces allowance before _move can return false for insufficient balance, so a failed transfer still consumes the caller's allowance.
When rewards are active with no stakers, this divides by zero, so calls such as the first stake or a reward update revert until someone stakes or the reward period ends.
Dividing before scaling truncates fractional reward-per-token increments to zero, so small rewards or large stake supplies can accrue no rewards at all.
The first stake leaves lockEnd at zero, so a user can immediately withdraw their entire initial stake without the advertised seven-day lock.
The external token transfer happens before the user's stake is cleared, so a recipient hook can reenter emergencyWithdraw and withdraw the same stake repeatedly from the pool.
The reward transfer's false return value is ignored after the user's rewards are cleared, so an underfunded pool can silently erase accrued rewards without paying them.
The signed voucher has no nonce or used-voucher tracking, so its recipient can submit the same valid signature repeatedly and receive the bonus multiple times.
Anyone can start or replace a reward epoch, allowing an arbitrary caller to disrupt the owner's schedule and control how the pool's reward balance is distributed.
If stakingToken and rewardToken are the same token, this balance check counts staked principal as available rewards, allowing a reward epoch and claims to consume tokens needed for withdrawals.
Replacing an active epoch sets the new rate using only the new reward amount and discards the previous epoch's unelapsed allocation, leaving those funds unaccounted for and potentially stranded.
Resetting the global reward index leaves users' paid checkpoints unchanged, so a later earned() call can underflow in its unchecked subtraction and produce bogus rewards or make claims fail.

raw_findings.message: `transferFrom` deducts allowance before `_move` checks the balance, so an underfunded call returns `false` but still consumes the caller's allowance.
When rewards are active while `totalSupply` is zero, any call that updates rewards after time has elapsed divides by zero here and can block the first stake until the reward period ends.
This divides before applying the 1e18 scale, so when `dt * rewardRate < totalSupply` the increment truncates to zero and stakers receive no rewards for that interval.
The first stake leaves `lockEnd` at zero, allowing a user to withdraw their entire initial stake immediately despite the documented seven-day lockup.
Emergency withdrawal changes the reward denominator without checkpointing elapsed rewards first, so the remaining stakers receive rewards calculated retroactively using the reduced supply.
The token transfer invokes the recipient hook before the user's balance and total supply are reduced, allowing a hooked staker to reenter `emergencyWithdraw` and withdraw the same stake repeatedly.
The return value is ignored after the user's reward balance is cleared, so an underfunded reward token can return `false` and silently erase the user's claim.
Because anyone can call `claimFor`, an attacker can trigger settlement before the user updates a stale payout address, irreversibly sending the user's rewards to that old address.
The signed voucher has no nonce or used-voucher tracking, so anyone can submit the same valid signature repeatedly to claim the bonus multiple times.
Anyone can start or replace a reward epoch, including setting a zero reward or changing the rate and finish time, so an attacker can disrupt the pool's scheduled rewards.
When the staking and reward tokens are the same, this balance check counts staked principal as available rewards, allowing reward payouts to drain funds needed for withdrawals.
Replacing an active epoch overwrites its rate without carrying forward its undistributed rewards, leaving the old epoch's remaining funds stranded in the pool.
Resetting the global reward-per-token value without resetting users' checkpoints makes `earned` underflow on the next epoch and can produce bogus rewards or make claims revert.

A transfer to `address(0)` succeeds and makes the tokens permanently inaccessible instead of rejecting the transfer, contrary to ERC-20 transfer behavior.

When an epoch elapses with zero stake, reward-per-token does not account for those emissions and later updates advance `lastUpdateTime`, leaving the corresponding reward tokens unallocated with no recovery path.
Because `notifyRewardAmount` is not restricted to the owner, anyone can alter an active reward schedule or start an epoch that expires before stakers arrive, disrupting or stranding rewards.
